## Rationale
Evaluates Bayesian probability: six strengths listed, but three specific problems (does not solve dependency, inappropriate priors for normative questions, qualitative evidence requires unobserved modeling assumptions), concluding 'excellent inference engine, not sufficient as the entire evidence model' — CANDIDATE FOR STATISTICAL CONTEXT. [S0893]

Evaluates Dempster-Shafer theory: the Bel≤Pl interval usefully represents incomplete knowledge without forcing precision, but strong conflict can behave problematically under some combination rules and source dependence is not automatically resolved — CANDIDATE FOR UNCERTAINTY CONTEXT. [S0893]

Evaluates the qualitative/set-based algebra A(H)=(S_H,C_H,U_H,L_H), naturally handling six epistemic states (Unknown/Supported/Challenged/Conflicted/Superseded/Retracted) but insufficient for quantitative probability/utility questions alone — designated the PRIMARY KERNEL CANDIDATE. [S0893]

Rejects weighted scoring as the kernel: a +5/-5 pair collapsing to score=0 destroys the crucial 'strong evidence on both sides' distinction (WeightedScore≠EpistemicState), REJECTED AS KERNEL though usable inside Sārathi for prioritization/ranking. [S0893]

Evaluates fuzzy logic as useful for vague concepts (architecture compatibility, capability maturity) but explicitly μ_H≠P(H), and fails to solve seven core requirements — not the kernel. [S0893]

Delivers a ten-requirement traffic-light comparison table across five candidates, with the qualitative approach scoring green on Unknown/Conflict/Provenance/Dependency while Bayesian and Dempster-Shafer score amber/red on those (noting provenance/dependency can be attached externally but is not automatic). [S0893]

Argues (via four contrasting example propositions — observational, normative, statistical, causal) that Evidence is more fundamental than any individual inference framework, called probably the most important conclusion of 25C.1. [S0893]
